lesson.title: ICMP: The Internet's Error Reporting Channel
lesson.summary: ICMP is a network layer protocol that routers and hosts use to report problems with IP packet delivery and to carry diagnostic messages, rather than to carry ordinary application data.
lesson.body:
IP itself is deliberately simple. Routers forward packets on a best effort basis and do not promise delivery, and if something goes wrong along the way, IP has no built in way to tell anyone about it. A router that has to drop a packet because it cannot find a route, or because the packet has been bouncing around too long, just drops it silently unless some other mechanism steps in to report the failure. That mechanism is the Internet Control Message Protocol, or ICMP.

ICMP messages travel inside IP packets, using their own protocol number in the IP header, but they are not really user data. They are short, structured reports that a router or host generates about the health of packet delivery: a network unreachable, a host unreachable, a packet that exceeded its time to live, a packet that arrived but was too large for the next link to carry. Each ICMP message carries a type field and a code field that together identify exactly what happened. Type 3, for example, covers destination unreachable conditions, with codes distinguishing an unreachable network from an unreachable host or an unreachable port. Type 11 reports that a packet's time to live counter hit zero before it reached its destination. Type 8 and type 0 are the echo request and echo reply messages that ping relies on, which the next chapter covers in detail.

Like every other piece of standardized internet behavior, ICMP's exact message formats and rules are not a matter of convention or folklore. They are pinned down in an RFC document, RFC 792 for ICMP as used with IPv4, so that every vendor's router and every operating system's network stack generates and interprets these messages the same way. Without that shared, written specification, a time exceeded message from a Cisco router might mean something different to a Linux host than the same message from a Juniper router, and diagnostic tools built on top of ICMP would be unreliable.

It is worth being clear about what ICMP is not. It has no port numbers and no concept of a connection, so it is not a transport protocol like TCP or UDP, and applications do not send their data over it. Its job is narrower and more specific: it is the feedback channel that lets the network layer talk about itself, reporting failures and conditions back to the sender of a packet so that hosts, routers, and the humans running diagnostic tools can understand what is happening underneath the surface of ordinary traffic. IPv6 uses a related but separate protocol, ICMPv6, which keeps the same error reporting role and also takes on extra duties that IPv4 handled with a completely different protocol, ARP, as later chapters on NDP will show.
